1	# OrcaSlicer features the AI has no tool for
2	
3	Handover written 2026-11-20. This is a working document: keep it untracked and don't commit it.
4	
5	## Summary
6	
7	A user asked JusPrin's AI to add filament changes at a list of heights. The AI said he would have to do it himself in the preview. It was right: OrcaSlicer stores these changes, but none of the AI's tools reads or writes them.
8	
9	Going through the AI's tool list turned up four more OrcaSlicer features in the same position. A person can do each of them by hand, but the AI can't do any of them. Nothing here is agreed or built. Each gap below is a proposal for Kenneth to decide on.
10	
11	## How it was found
12	
13	Bryan Duncan, a JusPrin 2.0.0 user on Linux with an Elegoo CC2 and its multi-filament unit, reported it by email on 2026-11-20 (Gmail thread `1a1f4a1831640907`).
14	
15	He is printing a large diorama made of many parts. The designer published files with the color changes already set for other printers, but not for the CC2. The designer did list, for each plate, the heights where the filament should change. Entering those by hand on the preview's layer slider is slow and tedious.
16	
17	Bryan gave the AI the heights and filaments. The AI understood the request but told him to use the preview. A support reply has already gone to him (sent 2026-11-20 16:36 Pacific). It said we would look into why the AI sent him to the preview.
18	
19	## What the AI can do today
20	
21	The tools are defined in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`. The AI can:
22	
23	- **Settings:** change settings for the whole print, a filament, the printer, or one whole object (`settings_preview_patch` / `settings_apply_patch`; the `scope` is `process`, `filament`, `printer` or `object`).
24	- **Filament:** give a whole object a filament (`plate_layout`, the `extruder` field in an object row).
25	- **Placing:** move, scale and rotate objects (`object_place`), and add plates, move objects between them and arrange them (`plate_layout`).
26	- **Shape edits:** cut an object along a plane, split it into its shells, merge, and repair (`object_divide`, `object_merge`, `object_repair`).
27	- **Marking faces:** mark faces for where the seam and supports should and shouldn't go (`region_annotate`).
28	- **Printing:** slice, read the result, run calibration prints, and export.
29	
30	## The gaps
31	
32	They're listed in the order of usefulness I'd guess. I haven't measured that order (see "Not verified").
33	
34	### 1. Changes at a height on a plate: filament change, pause, custom G-code
35	
36	This is Bryan's case. It also covers "pause at 12.4 mm so I can drop in magnets".
37	
38	- **Where the data lives:** `Model::plates_custom_gcodes` (`src/libslic3r/Model.hpp:1743`) maps each plate index to a `CustomGCode::Info`.
39	  - `CustomGCode::Info` (`src/libslic3r/CustomGCode.hpp:68`) is a list of `Item`s. Each `Item` holds `print_z`, a `type`, `extruder`, `color` and `extra`.
40	  - The `type` is `ColorChange`, `PausePrint`, `ToolChange`, `Template` or `Custom`.
41	- **How a person adds one:** right-click on the preview's layer slider, `IMSlider::add_code_as_tick` (`src/slic3r/GUI/IMSlider.hpp:145`).
42	- **Trap:** the slider holds its own copy of the list.
43	  - When a person edits a tick, `Plater.cpp:8210` overwrites the model's list for the current plate with the slider's ticks.
44	  - The slider reloads from the model in `Preview::update_layers_slider` (`src/slic3r/GUI/GUI_Preview.cpp:600`).
45	  - So a tool that writes the model must also refresh the slider. Otherwise the next tick edit by the person silently throws away what the AI wrote.
46	- **Snapping:** ticks sit on layer heights. A tool that takes a height in millimetres needs to decide how it snaps to a layer. That probably means the plate must be sliced first, or the tool works out the layer heights itself. This is undecided.
47	- **Not checked:** which `type` the slider uses for a single-nozzle printer with a multi-filament unit like the CC2 (`ToolChange` or `ColorChange`). Check it in the app before designing the tool.
48	- **Saved in the project already:** the 3MF writer and reader already store this list (`src/libslic3r/Format/bbs_3mf.cpp`), so no format change should be needed.
49	
50	### 2. A different filament for each part of one object
51	
52	An object can be made of several parts (`ModelVolume`). Today the AI can only set the filament of a whole object. A person sets it per part in the object list. Bryan's diorama is exactly this shape of model.
53	
54	Data: each `ModelVolume` has its own config, which can carry `extruder`.
55	
56	### 3. Settings for a height range of an object
57	
58	This is OrcaSlicer's height range modifier, for example "from 40 mm up, use 30% infill". The settings tools' `object` scope covers only the whole object.
59	
60	Data: `ModelObject::layer_config_ranges` (`src/libslic3r/Model.hpp:397`).
61	
62	### 4. Painting filament by height
63	
64	OrcaSlicer's color painting tool can fill every face between two heights with one filament. This works for a model that is one solid piece, where gap 2 doesn't apply.
65	
66	Data: `ModelVolume::mmu_segmentation_facets` (`src/libslic3r/Model.hpp:913`). This involves geometry, so I'd expect it to cost more than gaps 1 to 3.
67	
68	### 5. Modifiers and negative parts
69	
70	- A modifier is a box, cylinder or other shape inside an object whose space gets its own settings, for example denser infill around a screw hole.
71	- A negative part removes material, for example a hole for a nut.
72	
73	Data: `ModelVolumeType::PARAMETER_MODIFIER` and `NEGATIVE_VOLUME` (`src/libslic3r/Model.hpp:355`), added with `ModelObject::add_volume`. This also involves geometry: someone has to decide the shape's size and where it goes.
74	
75	## Not verified
76	
77	- I haven't checked how often other people ask the AI for any of these. Saved chats are the place to measure that before picking an order.
78	- I haven't checked Bryan's chat itself, so I don't know exactly what he typed or what the AI answered.
79	- I haven't checked whether the AI's guide (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/skills/`) tells people how to do any of these by hand. The only filament instruction I found covers choosing a whole object's filament.
80	
81	## Rules that apply to whoever builds this
82	
83	- Read `AGENTS.md`, including its error-handling section.
84	- The tool must not ask the person to approve the call. Tools run without approval.
85	- Wording the model reads calls the product "the app".
86	- Any change outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, such as the slider refresh in gap 1, follows `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`.
87

# JusPrin production documentation

This directory is the canonical starting point for production work on `jusprin-dev`. It preserves the durable product and engineering decisions from `jusprin-v2-poc` without importing the POC's temporary windows, probes, static mocks, generated evidence, or environment-gated startup paths.

Read these documents in order:

1. [Product definition](product-definition.md) — the human/agent boundary, required product surfaces, workflow, and visibility rules.
2. [Production architecture](architecture.md) — the selected native/WebView architecture, ownership rules, component boundaries, and implementation sequence.
3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.
7. [Design guidelines](design-guidelines.md) — how a screen gets designed and checked, the cold-reader check, and the wording rule for on-screen text.
8. [POC reference](poc-reference.md) — exact pointers to the spike-only documents, code, commits, logs, screenshots, and generated brand artifacts left on `jusprin-v2-poc`.
9. [Tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) — shared Agent/MCP contracts, process-settings workflow, execution and verification requirements.
10. [Local autosave and version history](autosave-version-history.md) — managed project storage, migration, restore, export, retention, and failure behavior.
11. [Writing a connection skill](connection-skill-guide.md) — what a printer-connection skill is for, the three audits before writing one, how to label what it states, and how to test it with a stuck person.

Printer UI without hardware (Bambu in-process fake; control file; isolated app): [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md). Moonraker and OctoPrint without hardware (Docker, real host software, simulated boards): [print hosts README](../../tests/printer_hosts/README.md).

## Governing decisions

- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
- When logic could live in either C++ or a React page, it goes in the page unless there is a strong reason for C++: it touches Orca state, enforces a limit or boundary the app must guarantee, has to work without a page, or needs a thread or lifetime the page lacks. See [Where logic goes](architecture.md#where-logic-goes-the-page-first).
- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and starting consequential physical actions.
- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.

## Source lineage

`jusprin-newui` and `jusprin-v2-poc` share base commit `8500fcdcca` (`v2.4.2`). `jusprin-dev` continues `jusprin-newui` and `ui-walkthrough`: it starts at `975c703f08`, the merge of OrcaSlicer 2.5.0, and contains both. The POC reference is pinned to final POC commit `9bba835b92`, so future changes to branch names do not make the historical evidence ambiguous.

1	# Guide for adding JusPrin tools
2	
3	**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.
4	
5	JusPrin has one tool system. A new capability is defined once, in the shared registry. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs it. Its implementation reads and changes the open project through the typed workspace interface. Two adapters, one for OpenAI and one for MCP, only translate that single definition into the format each side expects. The aim of this guide is a tool catalog that stays small, does only what it claims to do, can change safely over time, and is shaped by real printing tasks. It should not be shaped by a list of every feature OrcaSlicer has.
6	
7	Treat this guide as the starting point. Change it when what you learn from implementing, from real MCP clients, or from evals shows that a rule, a contract, a limit, or a sequence here should change. Do not keep a planning assumption just because it is written here. Base every revision on evidence, and describe significant changes in the PR. Two things do not change: OrcaSlicer stays the owner of the state it owns, and the verification requirements stay.
8	
9	Before you touch any OrcaSlicer class that holds live state, read [the production documentation](README.md), [production architecture](architecture.md), and [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). The current tool definitions are in [`ToolRegistry.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp). The code that runs them is in [`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp). The code that presents them over MCP is in [`McpProtocol.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp).
10	
11	External clients on the same machine connect through the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper, which is set up from **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and the server inside the app are compiled from the same registry. So every new tool you offer must have the same catalog entry and the same schema whether the app is running (live) or not (offline), for the same build and the same negotiated protocol version. Do not add a catalog that exists in only one adapter. Connecting to the server directly over HTTP is a route for developers. It is not what the default setup instructions tell people to do.
12	
13	## Words this guide uses
14	
15	- **Registry.** The one list of tool definitions, compiled into the app (`ToolRegistry.cpp`).
16	- **Catalog.** The list of tools as a caller sees it.
17	- **Coordinator.** `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, the class that queues tool calls and runs them on the GUI thread.
18	- **Workspace.** The typed C++ interface (`IWorkspace`) through which JusPrin reads and changes the open project. It has two implementations, called workspace adapters. The real one works on live OrcaSlicer. The fake one is for tests.
19	- **Tool adapter.** Code that translates registry definitions and results for one kind of caller. There are two: the in-app adapter, which uses OpenAI's format and serves the Agent panel, and the MCP adapter, which serves external clients. "Both adapters" in this guide means these two.
20	- **Projection.** The form in which one tool adapter presents a definition or a result.
21	- **Exposure.** The registry setting that says which callers are offered a tool.
22	- **Owner.** The OrcaSlicer class that holds the real copy of some state, or that already implements an operation.
23	- **Seam.** A small addition to a file OrcaSlicer owns, which lets fork code call or observe OrcaSlicer's behavior.
24	- **Session and revision.** `sessionId` identifies the project that is currently open. `revision` is a counter the workspace raises when its state changes. A call that was prepared against an older session or revision is called stale.
25	- **Action class.** Whether a tool is read-only, a mutation (it changes something), or destructive.
26	- **Dirty.** A preset is dirty when it has unsaved edits.
27	- **Eval.** An automated test that gives a model a task and checks the transcript that results.
28	- **M0 to M5.** The milestones in which the tool catalog was delivered.
29	
30	## Current connection and execution boundary
31	
32	- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
33	- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
34	- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
35	- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
36	- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
37	- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
38	- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.
39	
40	Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.
41	
42	A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".
43	
44	## Start with an eval failure
45	
46	The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.
47	
48	Write down:
49	
50	- what the user wanted to achieve;
51	- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
52	- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
53	- what a successful transcript should look like;
54	- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
55	- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.
56	
57	If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.
58	
59	The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.
60	
61	## Decide whether this should be a tool
62	
63	Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.
64	
65	Do not add a tool for:
66	
67	- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
68	- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
69	- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
70	- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
71	- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
72	- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
73	- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.
74	
75	A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
76	
77	## Skills versus tools
78	
79	A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
80	
81	- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
82	- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
83	
84	The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
85	
86	A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
87	
88	- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
89	- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
90	- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
91	- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.
92	
93	A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists. One skill has a description and a trigger: `calibration`, read when a print problem may come from the filament or its settings, when the person asks to calibrate, or in a calibration project, and fired by `calibration_started` on the first turn of a calibration project's chat; it carries the conversation of a calibration (when a test is worth it, the two facts said before the person's project closes, asking which test only when the handover leaves it open, per-test ranges and how to read the print, the naming rule for the saved preset), while `calibration_generate`'s description keeps only that tool's rules. Four other skills have triggers, one file each:
94	
95	- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96	- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed it (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that restates the same purpose, or leaves it out, to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded, and on every turn's first request while the plan is marked `needs_reassessment` (2026-10-28: the model may leave recording the plan to the turn that answers its question about the change, and that turn finds the setup checked already, so without this the mark could outlive every skill that explains it). Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97	- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98	- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's Ask AI button asks for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists. The chip and `slice_report` read the same slice-result rule (`Workspace/SliceResultWarnings`), so they list the same warnings, except that `slice_report` also lists the timelapse ones, marked `appliesWhen: "timelapse"`, which the chip does not count. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
99	
100	The connection skills (`connect-bambu`, and `connect-print-host` for every print host type) have rules of their own, in [Writing a connection skill](connection-skill-guide.md).
101	
102	The cases in between:
103	
104	- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
105	- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
106	- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
107	- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
108	
109	When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
110	
111	How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
112	
113	## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs
114	
115	The settings workflow has four operations that do not change. They work on searchable data, whichever preset layer the values belong to:
116	
117	```text
118	settings_search → settings_get → settings_preview_patch → settings_apply_patch
119	```
120	
121	Do not create one tool per setting:
122	
123	```text
124	set_layer_height
125	set_wall_loops
126	set_infill_density
127	set_support_angle
128	```
129	
130	The same rule applies to presets, project objects, plates, warnings, and slice reports. Extend the typed records that describe them, and the size-limited tools that query them, before you create dozens of special-purpose actions.
131	
132	A new operation deserves its own tool when it really differs from the existing ones in at least one of these ways: which action class it belongs to (read-only, mutation or destructive), whether it applies completely or not at all, how it starts, runs, and ends, or what its result means. `slice_start` is an example. It is not one more way to change settings. It starts OrcaSlicer work that runs in the background, and it completes in a different way from a settings change. That difference justifies a separate tool.
133	
134	Split an operation into a preview tool and an apply tool only where OrcaSlicer may rewrite, replace, or refuse what the caller asked for. In those cases the caller has to see what would really happen before submitting the change. There are three such cases:
135	
136	- settings, because OrcaSlicer's normalizer (the code that adjusts dependent settings after an edit) can rewrite values;
137	- preset selection, because OrcaSlicer may substitute a compatible preset, and dirty edits may be lost;
138	- topology changes such as cutting, splitting, or merging, because the caller needs to see the resulting pieces.
139	
140	Sending a print is not a fourth. The agent opens OrcaSlicer's send dialog, which shows the person the slot mapping and the printer's readiness, and the person presses Send there (see [Sending a print](product-definition.md#29-sending-a-print)).
141	
142	Everywhere else, the coordinator computes and validates the resulting state as part of the call. If a preview would only repeat its input back, do not make it a tool.
143	
144	Prefer read tools whose results have a fixed, typed shape. Avoid one general record search whose result changes shape. Each section of `workspace_inspect` keeps its own fixed shape. A generic `records_search` whose result shape depends on a `kind` argument would make the model guess what comes back.
145	
146	## Tool budget and tool shape
147	
148	The limit on the number of tools comes from how much the model has to load on each turn. It does not come from how much the app can do. The rules in this section rest on this evidence:
149	
150	- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
151	- Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools aimed at high-impact workflows. It names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error.
152	- A [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured three interfaces. A generic interface of thin tools scored below raw SQL. Tools shaped around the domain scored far above both.
153	- The "god tool", one tool that dispatches many unrelated actions through a single `action` parameter, is a documented anti-pattern.
154	
155	The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, and two thirds of that is output schema.
156	
157	**How tools are loaded for now.** Both adapters load every registered tool on every turn. The in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest behaviour that is correct. It also keeps the tools array byte-identical through a chat, and OpenAI's prompt cache depends on exactly that. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements. The live regression test records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request. The journey catalog below goes over 20 definitions from its first milestone. We accept that until those measurements show the model selecting wrong tools or running short of context.
158	
159	**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**
160	
161	| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
162	|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
163	| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
164	| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
165	| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
166	| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
167	| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
168	| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |
169	
170	The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.
171	
172	The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.
173	
174	The conclusion is that a definition adds cost to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn. That is why going over the budget only makes us look at the measurements and does not block a tool. Two things would change this conclusion: a catalog so large that the first request of every conversation is expensive by itself, or transcripts that show the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch for both. Neither has appeared yet.
175	
176	**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.
177	
178	One tool is added during a conversation, on purpose. `issue_report_open` comes with either connection skill, `connect-bambu` or `connect-print-host` (`PrinterConversation::connection_skill`, carried as `AgentSkillUse::tools`). It is offered from the request where the skill is first sent, including the continuation after the tool result that brought the skill, and on every request after that. The skill, and so the tool, comes into force once the chat has a saved printer: with `printer_add`'s result, or on the first request of a chat about one. A chat with no saved printer never has it. Adding it costs that chat one prompt-cache miss, and that cost was accepted. The list stays the same from then on. This is not deferral: no tool search, no `defer_loading`, and no toolsets. The app decides when the tool is offered, and the model never asks for it.
179	
180	What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:
181	
182	- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
183	- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one. When the project uses that printer, its unsaved edits are dropped and listed in `discarded`; the panel's coordinator saves a version first, as the project's agent pane does for any change to the project. If that save fails, the call does not run and returns the coordinator's generic `local_save_failed`; there is no separate message for it.
184	- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
185	- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.
186	
187	A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.
188	
189	The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.
190	
191	We do not give each mode a different tool list, for two reasons. The conversation has to refuse disallowed calls anyway, whatever list the model is shown. And the way to restrict tools while keeping the list stable (`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. We would reconsider if transcripts showed the model reaching for a refused tool and then failing to recover. `tests/printer_prompt` measures this with the `change-add-another` case.
192	
193	Two past changes explain the current design:
194	
195	- Until 2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07). The reason was to keep a printer lookup from clearing the pinned card of the printer a Change session was about. That card is gone (4d4f9e466b). Offering one tool per step also left an Add conversation with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b).
196	- On 2026-09-28 three tools were removed (b60fc2d8e6): `printer_manual_setup`, `printer_manual_connection` and `printer_setup_finish`. These were the tools that opened a window or closed the panel. The full printer list (the printer form since 2026-10-20, or OrcaSlicer's own list when the panel's page cannot load) and a printer's settings are still reachable from the panel's own buttons, and the person closes the panel.
197	
198	The app decides which tools are offered. The page writes the text: `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` holds the instructions, and `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` holds the notes the model reads after a tap. If a turn arrives before the page has written its instructions, the app refuses the turn. The app has no prompt of its own to send instead. The instructions for an Add conversation carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB. That text is always the same and sits at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace state goes into the turn, and none goes into a tool result.
199	
200	**Deferral, when the measurements say so.** Deferral means the model first sees only a short index and loads a tool's full definition when it needs it. Use the deferral feature that the model platform provides. Never write our own mechanism for switching tools in and out. For the in-app Agent, the platform feature is OpenAI's `tool_search` with `defer_loading: true` on the Responses API. It is documented for `gpt-5.4` and later. Whether it works on the pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` has not been verified. On the MCP side, clients defer by themselves, as Claude Code does. Tools would be deferred one toolset at a time (toolsets are the named groups in the candidate catalog), and OpenAI recommends fewer than ten functions per namespace. Do not build a tool that enables a toolset by rewriting the tools array. Every switch would break the prompt cache.
201	
202	**Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing that a slicer user has a name for: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Do not wrap each OrcaSlicer function in its own tool. Do not build a tool that interprets a list of unrelated commands. One operation may have several optional facets, as long as each facet has its own type and the tool rejects facets that conflict.
203	
204	**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.
205	
206	**Fold reads into sections and detail levels before adding a read tool.** A new read tool is justified in only two cases. Either its inputs are of a different kind (a search over a large catalog, an analysis of one object, a report on a sliced plate), or its result is an image.
207	
208	**Let call logs decide consolidation.** If transcripts show that two tools are always called together, consider merging them. If two facets of one tool are never used together, consider splitting them. Make these decisions from eval evidence, not from a design discussion.
209	
210	**Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` no longer carries `outputSchema`. `validate_output` still checks every successful MCP result, so a result that breaks its contract still fails with a visible error. We measured the effect on one build, with the recipe near the end of this guide. With five tools, the catalog went from 9,723 bytes to 3,141, which is from about 2,430 tokens to 785. Only the MCP side saves anything. The in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn never carried output schemas. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.
211	
212	## Choose the narrowest honest scope
213	
214	Do not put an enum value in a schema, such as one of `printer | filament | process | object`, unless every advertised value works in both the fake and the real workspace adapter and inherits values the way the documentation says.
215	
216	For each proposed capability, answer:
217	
218	1. Which OrcaSlicer owner holds the real state or performs the operation?
219	2. Is the command valid for the whole project, one plate, one object, one instance, or one preset layer?
220	3. What stable ID identifies the target, and when does that ID expire?
221	4. Which revision must still be current when the command executes?
222	5. Which existing OrcaSlicer undo snapshot covers the change, and how is the change undone, reset, or reverted? Or does ordinary project Undo not apply?
223	6. Which workspace change reasons tell readers that they must read again?
224	7. What happens if the user edits something in the GUI while the call is queued or running?
225	
226	If any of these answers is unclear, the tool's contract is not ready.
227	
228	## Reuse the one authority path
229	
230	Every change to the project must take this route:
231	
232	```text
233	adapter call
234	→ shared registry validation
235	→ ToolExecutionCoordinator queue
236	→ immediate execution
237	→ IWorkspace command
238	→ current Orca owner
239	→ Orca history and state change
240	→ coalesced workspace event
241	→ fresh snapshot/result
242	```
243	
244	A tool adapter must not call `Plater`, `Model`, `PresetBundle`, wxWidgets, or slicing objects directly. Do not copy an OrcaSlicer operation into JusPrin. If the operation you need exists only inside OrcaSlicer's UI code, add the smallest possible seam to the class that currently owns the operation. Name the seam for what it does, and put nothing JusPrin-specific in it.
245	
246	Any change to a file OrcaSlicer owns must follow [fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Keep the diff small, and add lines instead of rewriting existing ones. Record why the seam belongs where you put it, identify the upstream lines you touched, and include the rebase evidence.

248	## JusPrin-owned project state
249	
250	Some product state is not held anywhere in OrcaSlicer: the print's purpose, the pinned agent plan, semantic region annotations, physical facts the user confirmed about a printer, and the monitoring rules the user sets for automatic pausing. For this state, the "current Orca owner" step in the route above is a JusPrin store instead. Every other step stays the same. The rules are:
251	
252	- **Storage.** State that belongs to a project (purpose, plan, regions, conversation, and attachments) lives in the local project store, under a project ID that does not change. The current `ProjectStateDocument` is saved separately from model checkpoints. An imported project may contain the older `Auxiliaries/JusPrin/state.json`. It is read only to migrate it. In that document:
253	  - each chat owns its purpose, the setup title `setupIntent` (with the purpose setup beside it), and its plan, `plan`. The project's current purpose and plan are the active chat's, read through `activeConversationId` and stored nowhere else; a new chat starts with a copy of the active chat's purpose and no plan. A plan write replaces the whole plan. A chat's `printIntent`, the requirement fields `setup_record` kept until 2026-10-25, is no longer read or copied; a document that holds one loads as before;
254	  - the region annotations, `regions`, describe the model in the workspace. A write replaces the whole list, and each record is stamped with a seq when it changes. Every saved model version records the list it was saved with, and restoring or resuming that version puts its list back.
255	
256	  State that belongs to a printer (confirmed facts, monitoring policy) stays in app data, stored per printer identity, the way `PrinterFactsStore` keeps it. Confirmed facts carry an expiry, because the physical world changes without telling the app. See [Local autosave and version history](autosave-version-history.md).
257	- **Revision.** Every write has to signal that it happened, so that readers read again. Two questions are still **open**: which signal to use, and whether the signal invalidates actions that are already queued. They belong to the milestone that adds the first writer. The obvious answer would be to publish a `WorkspaceChangeReasons` bit and add that bit to `kInvalidatingReasons`. That cannot be built as described. `settings_apply_patch` requires its caller's `expectedRevision` to equal the current revision exactly. So if the revision goes up at any point between a client's preview and its apply, the apply fails as `stale_workspace`. An agent that recorded its plan between previewing and applying would make its own call fail. There is an existing example of the alternative: the edit feed (`WorkspaceEditHub`) reports a change without raising the revision. Decide separately for each kind of state. A region annotation generates OrcaSlicer artifacts, so it is a real change to the project. A purpose, or a statement of the plan, is not. In the code as built, writing a region record signals nothing by itself. The artifacts it generates are ordinary OrcaSlicer edits, and they raise the revision in the usual way. So an action that was queued before an annotation goes stale, exactly as it would after any other edit to the model.
258	- **Undo.** None of this state is in OrcaSlicer's undo stack. Results say `projectUndo: false`. Region annotations are the awkward case. They generate OrcaSlicer artifacts (modifier volumes, enforcers, blockers, paint), and those artifacts *are* in the undo stack. So project Undo can leave an annotation without its artifacts, or leave an artifact without its annotation. The `regions` section of `object_analyze` reports both situations, and `region_annotate` generates the artifacts again. The result of a place, divide, or repair lists the regions whose link to the geometry that operation broke.
259	- **Provenance (where a value came from).** Any field that records a fact about the world or about what the user wants also records its source: `file` (read from the project or a profile), `observed` (reported by a sensor or the printer, with a timestamp), `agent_inferred`, or `user_confirmed`. A tool marks a value `user_confirmed` only when the call is based on something the user explicitly said. Values the agent inferred stay `agent_inferred`. A value only the model writes, with nothing in the app that confirms it, cannot be `user_confirmed`: `setup_record`'s requirement fields were stored that way and fed back to the model each turn as the person's facts, and were removed on 2026-10-25. When a tool reads printer state, it reports the `configured` value and the `observed` value of the same fact separately, and it computes the `mismatches` between them itself. That comparison is not left to the model.

507	
508	This catalog lists the tools the finished product would have. It was worked out one product screen at a time from [Designing an AI-Piloted OrcaSlicer](orca-feature-discovery.md), and shaped by the rules under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape). Nothing in it is implemented unless the catalog record above says so. Every row still needs what this guide requires of any tool: the eval failure, the trace of its owner, and the test matrix. The number that matters is how many definitions load per turn, not the total. The total here is 34. All of them load on every turn until the measurements under [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape) justify deferral. The toolsets below are the groups that would be deferred together when that day comes. Until then they only group tools for naming and for delivery.

510	These conventions apply to every row:
511	
512	- Every read returns `sessionId` and `revision`.
513	- Every write that is revision-sensitive takes `expectedRevision`.
514	- A handle for a detected face or hole carries the revision it was computed at. After the revision moves, using the handle fails with `feature_expired`.
515	- Facts carry provenance, as defined under [JusPrin-owned project state](#jusprin-owned-project-state).
516	- Long-running rows follow [Asynchronous operations](#asynchronous-operations). They return an action handle, and the handle's state is read from the `slicing` section of `workspace_inspect`.
517	- Every read states a fixed maximum size and has a flag that says when the result was cut short.

519	In the Class column, **R** means read-only, **M** means mutation, and **D** means destructive.

643	### Deliberately not tools
644	
645	These will not be tools:
646	
647	- one tool per setting, or one per bundle such as "make it stronger";
648	- printing advice;
649	- preferences, cloud, firmware, plugins, sync, and installing updates. These belong to the user, according to surface 2.12 of the product definition;
650	- manual axis movement, homing, detailed fan and light control, and printer file storage. These belong to the expert layer of Monitor;
651	- painting stroke by stroke, and the measure gizmo as a UI. The model reaches the same results through regions and through the handles that analysis returns;

### Scope expansion acceptance criteria

- The registry offers the same required `scope` enum and the same target
  shape through the in-app adapter and the MCP adapter. Catalog tests pin
  both projections.
- Argument tests reject an omitted or unknown scope, and every target that is
  missing, extra, zero-based, mixed, or malformed. No test accepts the old
  call shape.
- Search, get, preview, and apply are each covered against the fake and the
  real workspace adapter, for all four scopes, including a key that can be
  read but not written.
- Filament tests cover three cases: a preset in a slot that is not open in
  its tab, a copy taking the original's slot, and a save that drops the
  unsaved edits of the filament open in the tab.
- Printer tests prove that changing a normal writable value updates the
  native field, the dirty marker, the slice invalidation, and the value read
  back. They also prove that the topology keys and the compatibility keys
  stay unwritable.
- Apply tests prove four things: a failed apply changes nothing, the activity
  text is right for each scope, a preset change can be reverted or reversed
  with an inverse patch, and project Undo applies only to object overrides.
- Evals and the deterministic agent's fixtures use explicit scopes before the
  old schema is removed. There is no phase in which both schemas are
  accepted.

### Error codes
----
### Per-object overrides

A read with `scope: "object"` and `target: {"objectId": "..."}` returns the
value the object prints with. That is the object's own override where its
`ModelConfig` has one (`overridden: true`), and the process value otherwise.

A patch is checked against the process config with the object's overrides and
the patch applied on top. The checks are the same as for a process patch:
parsing, bounds, the conditions that would open a dialog, the support style
rule, and `Slic3r::validate`. A key that is neither a `PrintRegionConfig`
option nor a `PrintObjectConfig` option is refused with `unsupported_scope`.
That is ObjectList's own list for a whole object. No dependencies are
predicted. OrcaSlicer runs the normalizer only on the process preset and on
edits made in the object settings panel, so an override is stored as written.

Apply does the following:

1. takes one `Plater::TakeSnapshot` ("Change object settings");
2. writes each key with `ModelConfig::set_key_value`;
3. calls `ObjectList::object_config_options_changed`, so that the list shows
   the settings item;
4. calls `Plater::changed_object`, so that the slicing of that object is
   invalidated.

The result says `projectUndo: true`, and project Undo removes the override.
The activity names the object. The coordinator looks the object up in the
current snapshot twice, when the action is queued and when it executes, and
fails with `not_found` when the object is gone. The adapter treats a
missing target as a broken precondition. No value in a patch removes an
override. Only Undo, or the object settings panel, does.

----
The user should judge that reasoning without having to configure every underlying value.

The full intent editor should appear during project creation, import, or when requirements are incomplete. Afterward, Prepare should retain only a compact editable summary. Specialized questions such as food contact, flexibility, critical clearances, and protected support surfaces should appear contextually rather than in every project.

---

## 2.4 Objects, parts, and plates

This surface answers: **What exactly is included in this job?**

OrcaSlicer’s object and plate tree is essential, although its presentation can be simplified.

### What should remain

- Every plate in the project
- Every object and part
- Object names
- Quantity and duplicates
- Which objects are enabled
- Which material or extruder each object uses
- Modifiers, support enforcers, and support blockers
- Object-specific requirements
- Print order where it matters
- Search for complex projects

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

The agent cannot assume that every imported object should be printed or that apparently duplicated parts are accidental. A modifier may encode engineering intent that is invisible in the rendered outer surface.

Multi-plate organization can also represent batches, material differences, alternative versions, or assembly groups.

### What the agent should do

Arrange objects, detect accidental overlaps, identify likely duplicates, balance plates, and suggest grouping—but show the resulting job manifest for confirmation.

----
## 2.6 Local meaning and region-level overrides

This surface answers: **Are different parts or surfaces subject to different requirements?**

Global instructions such as “make it strong” are often insufficient.

### What should remain

Users need ways to identify:

- Faces that must remain smooth
- Surfaces where support contact is allowed or forbidden
- Precision holes and mating surfaces
- Areas requiring additional strength
- Flexible or sacrificial regions
- Visible versus hidden faces
- Preferred or forbidden seam locations
- Different material or color regions
- Areas where texture is intentional
- Object-specific print requirements

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

Computer vision can estimate geometry, but it cannot reliably know the functional role of every region.

For example, an agent may place a seam on the geometrically least visible face, unaware that the face mates with another part. It may strengthen the thickest region even though failure occurs around a small mounting hole.

### What the agent should do

Use semantic labels to generate modifiers and technical settings automatically. Users should describe meaning; they should not normally need to configure local speeds, wall counts, or infill percentages themselves.

---
----
- Supports that may be difficult to remove
- Supports entering holes, cavities, or mating regions
- A direct Adjust supports or Mark protected areas action that returns to Prepare

If no supports exist, Check should emphasize the most consequential detected risk instead.

- Seams on protected or visible surfaces
- Risky bridges and overhangs
- Thin or missing features
- First-layer contact problems
- Unsupported islands
- Unexpected gaps or collisions
- Material or color changes
- Purge volume and waste
- Prime tower and extruder assignments

content.text:
Yes for one of the five features, and mostly no for the rest. Changes at a height on a plate (a filament change, or a pause to drop in magnets) are a real gap that the tool guide's own test supports filling. For three of the other four, the handover missed that the existing region-marking tool already reaches part of them, so better tool text comes before new tools.

**What the guide asks for**

`agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md` says a tool starts from a transcript where the AI could not finish a real task, never from "OrcaSlicer has this feature". It also says to extend an existing tool before adding one, and to fix a description first when that would be enough. The handover has one such transcript, Bryan's, and nobody has read it yet. The other four features came from walking the tool list, which the guide names as the wrong starting point.

**Changes at a height on a plate: worth building**

No existing tool reads or writes them, and no modifier can express a pause. Three things I read in the code change the handover's picture:

- **No need to slice first.** The slicer matches each change to the nearest layer (`ToolOrdering::assign_custom_gcodes`), so a height in millimetres works as given.
- **Filament changes only apply to a one-filament plate.** When the objects on the plate already use more than one filament, the slicer ignores these changes without saying so (`ToolOrdering.cpp:3280`). The tool would have to report that.
- **Project Undo does not cover them.** The slider's edit takes no undo snapshot (`Plater.cpp:8206`).

The slider writes the type `ToolChange` when more than one filament is loaded (`IMSlider.cpp:1567`). That is from reading the code, not from running the app with a CC2.

My proposals, none agreed:

- Add the read first, as part of `workspace_inspect`. Today the AI cannot see changes a designer's file already carries.
- Make the write a field on the plate rows of `plate_layout`, not a new tool. The catalog already has 25 or more tools against a watch line of 20.
- Offer filament change and pause only. Arbitrary G-code at a height is a separate safety question, and I could not confirm whether the settings tools already refuse G-code settings.

**The other four**

- **Settings for a height range, filament by height on a solid model, and modifiers.** `region_annotate` already takes a box or cylinder in millimetres and creates a modifier with settings (`reinforce`) or with a filament (`material`). A box spanning a height band should cover the first two. That is my hypothesis and I have not run it. If it holds, the fix is a sentence in the tool description, which the guide prefers.
- **A different filament for each part of one object.** This is a real gap: `plate_layout` takes only an object id. It is small, because the workspace already reads each part's filament. I would extend an existing tool, and only once a transcript shows someone asking.
- **Negative parts.** No one has asked. The guide parks text embossing for the same reason, and this belongs with it.

**Still open**

- Bryan's actual chat and how often other people ask for any of these.
- An eval for these requests: I did not find one in `tests/project_prompt`, but I did not check exhaustively.
- Whether the AI's guide tells people how to do these by hand. The plates-and-objects page mentions parts and modifiers only in passing.

Did the brief just ask you to check the height related scenarios? If so, it's wrong. What I meant to ask you is to check all the features that the  OrcaSlicer, the upstream, currenlty offers that AI should be able to provide help with.

No. The handover covers five features, and only three of them are about height (changes at a height on a plate, settings for a height range, painting filament by height). But its scope is still far narrower than what you meant. Its author found the five by going through the AI's tool list and asking what sat next to each tool, and I checked those five and nothing else. Nobody has yet gone through OrcaSlicer's own feature list, which is what you're asking for.

I'm doing that now: an inventory of what upstream OrcaSlicer offers, taken from the upstream code this fork contains, set against every tool and skill the AI has.
